Q60779306.summary: This little pilgrim's flask, only 6.3 cm high, still has fragments of its leather strap. On the front, in low relief, the Crucifixion is shown in the Holy Land manner: a haloed Christ above the cross between the two thieves with outstretched arms, with kneeling figures at its foot. On the back is the Ascension: Christ enthroned in a mandorla borne by angels, above the Virgin and the apostles. A Greek inscription runs round each face. Filled with oil from the holy sites of Jerusalem, such flasks carried both blessing and image home to distant believers.
facts: It belongs to the 'Monza' or 'Bobbio' type, named after the Italian treasuries where the largest groups of these Palestinian ampullae survive; the Monza flasks were given by the Lombard queen Theodelinda (c. 570–628).
The flasks held oil from lamps burning before the great shrines of the Holy Land, and the oil was believed to heal the sick.
Their images come from a period that has left very few traces in art, yet was of crucial importance in establishing the iconography of many Christian subjects.
Q60779306.notes: Cleveland also catalogues the two faces separately as 1999.46.a (Crucifixion) and 1999.46.b (Ascension); those entries (Q60755446, Q60779637) are rejected as duplicates of this one. The inscriptions are only partly legible in the photographs and are not transcribed.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Under a row of arches, the haloed Christ stands holding a book among crowds of people who press toward him from either side. The psalm opens 'God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods', and the verse below calls to 'deliver the poor and needy'.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. Only the lower part of the miniature is fully visible at this resolution.

cur:monumental2-san-vincenzo-virgin-and-.summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a jewelled throne set within a large circular glory, with the Christ Child, golden-haloed, held before her; below, a row of saints' heads looks out. The full composition, of which this is the upper part, also includes a monk kneeling in adoration – a reminder of the community for whom the crypt was painted.
facts: The crypt combines images of Christ, the Virgin, the Annunciation and Nativity with the martyrdoms of Lawrence and Stephen, a programme focused on intercession for the abbot and his monks.
cur:monumental2-san-vincenzo-virgin-and-.notes: The kneeling monk mentioned in the Commons title is not visible in this crop.

cur:objects-petit-palais-virgin-child-en.summary: Beneath a pierced canopy the Virgin sits on a cushioned throne, holding the Christ Child frontally on her lap, while two small busts in medallions look on from the upper corners. The Child sits upright like a little emperor, blessing, the Lord enthroned in the lap of his Mother. The tall, slender proportions and delicate openwork are typical of the finest ivories of 10th-century Constantinople.
facts: The plaque is attributed to Constantinople around 950–1000, the period sometimes called the 'Macedonian Renaissance' of Byzantine ivory carving.
The Virgin enthroned with the Child seated frontally on her knees (the Kyriotissa type) presents Mary as the throne of Christ (type).

cur:objects-coin-leo-vi-constantine-vii-.summary: Christ sits frontally on a lyre-backed throne, blessing and holding the Gospels, encircled by the legend IHS XPS REX REGNANTIUM, 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. On the reverse Leo VI and his young son Constantine VII stand together holding a patriarchal cross. Christ enthroned as King of kings presides over the dynasty that his heavenly authority legitimised.
facts: Leo VI's earlier solidi (886–908) show the Virgin orans instead of Christ; the enthroned Christ appears on this joint issue with Constantine VII.
The same Christ enthroned with a lyre-backed throne appears in the mosaic over the Imperial Gate of Hagia Sophia, where Leo VI prostrates himself before Christ (comparison).
cur:objects-coin-leo-vi-constantine-vii-.notes: Leo VI's Virgin-orans solidus is documented by the CNG specimen 'Solidus of Leo VI.jpg' on Commons.
